subject: Science
source: National Curriculum KS2 Science (Earth and space; Forces); Drive Science 'Science lower school' (3.1 forces, 3.7 earth) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 9 to 18): Tarbiyyah Primary Year 5 Science Long Term Plan 2023-24 (Cornerstones Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats), home practicals with household items

lessons.title: The Solar System
objectives: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun
Describe the Sun as a star at the centre of our Solar System
Compare the planets using simple facts

keywords.def: a huge ball of hot, glowing gas, like the Sun
a large object that orbits a star
the curved path of one object around another
the Sun and everything that orbits it

starter: Bismillah. What are the three states of matter?
What gives us light and heat in the daytime?
Can you name any planets?

teach.heading: The Sun is a star
bullets: It gives us light and heat
teach.note: The Sun is the only star in our Solar System. It looks big because it is close; other stars are far away. Never look directly at the Sun.

teach.heading: Eight planets
teach.note: Teach a mnemonic. The inner four are rocky; Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants (an older teaching calls all four gas giants). Pluto is a dwarf planet.

teach.heading: Planet facts
bullets: Mercury is closest to the Sun
teach.note: Venus is hotter than Mercury because of its thick atmosphere. A common misconception is that the closest planet is hottest.

teach.heading: Moons and orbits
bullets: Planets take different times to orbit
teach.note: Earth takes about 365 days to orbit the Sun. Mercury takes 88 days; Neptune takes about 165 years. Link to Qur'an 21:33: the sun and moon float in orbits.

practice: Which planet is third from the Sun?
Which is the largest planet?
What does it mean to orbit?
independent: Draw the Solar System in order with each planet labelled.
Make a fact file for one planet with four facts.
Explain why Venus is hotter than Mercury.
exit: Name the planet we live on and its number from the Sun.
lessons.homework: Make a model of the Solar System with household items and name each planet.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a planet order strip with pictures. Stretch: compare the size of Earth and Jupiter using numbers (Jupiter's diameter is about 11 times Earth's).

lessons.title: Day and night
objectives: Explain that Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours
Use a model to explain day and night
Explain why the Sun seems to move across the sky

keywords.def: an imaginary line through the Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole
spinning around an axis
when the Sun first appears in the morning
when the Sun disappears in the evening

starter: Bismillah. Name the planet closest to the Sun.
Does the Sun move around the Earth or does the Earth move around the Sun?
What is an orbit?

teach.heading: Earth spins
teach.note: Hold a ball or globe with a torch. The half facing the torch has day, the other half has night. Misconception: the Sun goes around the Earth, or the Moon causes night.

teach.heading: Why the Sun seems to move
bullets: Sun appears to rise in the east
It appears to set in the west
teach.note: Explain the Sun only appears to move. Link to the five daily prayers: their times depend on the position of the Sun (fajr at dawn, dhuhr after midday, maghrib at sunset). Use with care.

teach.heading: Shadows through the day
bullets: Shadows are long in the morning
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: stand a pencil in plasticine on paper in a sunny spot and mark the shadow tip each hour. Never look at the Sun. Alternatively use a torch and a video.

teach.heading: Time around the world
bullets: When it is day here it is night elsewhere
Our class meets across time zones
teach.note: Great link for an online school: pupils in different countries have different local times. Ask where pupils are and what time it is for them.

practice: How long does the Earth take to spin once?
Which direction does the Sun appear to rise from?
Why is it night in a place facing away from the Sun?
independent: Draw the Earth with the Sun and shade the night side. Label day and night.
Explain in three sentences why the Sun seems to move across the sky.
Record shadow lengths in a table and draw a line graph.
lessons.homework: Mark your shadow outside at three different times of day, using chalk or string with a grown-up, and measure the lengths.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a torch and ball model and clear step-by-step diagram. Stretch: explain why the polar regions have very long days and nights.

lessons.title: The Moon and its phases
objectives: Describe the Moon as a natural satellite that orbits Earth
Name the phases of the Moon
Explain why the Moon seems to change shape

keywords.def: an object that orbits a larger object
the shape of the lit part of the Moon we can see
a thin curved sliver of light
about 29.5 days, the time from one new Moon to the next

starter: Bismillah. How long does Earth take to spin once?
What causes day and night?
Have you seen the Moon in the sky? What shape was it?

teach.heading: The Moon orbits Earth
bullets: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite
It takes about 27 days to orbit
It does not make its own light
teach.note: The Moon reflects sunlight. Misconception: the Moon makes light. Orbit around Earth takes 27.3 days; phase cycle is 29.5 days.

teach.heading: Phases
bullets: Waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous
teach.note: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. We see different amounts of the lit half as the Moon orbits. The phases are NOT caused by Earth's shadow. Common misconception.

teach.heading: Model the phases
teach.note: Safe demo: in a dark room with a lamp or torch, hold a ball at arm's length and turn slowly. Children see crescent, half and full. Or use a video of the model.

teach.heading: The Moon and the Islamic calendar
bullets: A month begins with the new crescent
Ramadan and Eid depend on the Moon
teach.note: Link to the Hijri calendar being lunar. Keep to facts: months start when the new crescent is sighted or calculated. Refer respectfully to how local scholars decide.

practice: Does the Moon make its own light?
Name two phases of the Moon.
How long is a lunar month?
independent: Draw the eight phases of the Moon in order and label them.
Use a ball and lamp (or video) and explain what causes a crescent Moon.
Write a fact file about the Moon with five facts.
exit: Why can we see the Moon?
Name one phase of the Moon.
lessons.homework: Look at the Moon tonight, or find a picture. Draw its shape and name the phase.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide phase pictures to sequence. Stretch: explain why we always see the same side of the Moon.

lessons.title: How ideas about the Solar System changed
objectives: Describe the geocentric and heliocentric models
Explain that scientists change ideas when new evidence is found
Name scientists, including Muslim scholars, who studied the sky

keywords.def: an idea that the Earth is at the centre
an idea that the Sun is at the centre
facts or observations that support an idea
an instrument that makes distant objects look closer

starter: Bismillah. Name the phases of the Moon you can remember.
What orbits the Sun?
Why does the Sun seem to move?

teach.heading: Earth at the centre
bullets: Ancient people thought Earth was central
The Sun and stars seem to go around us
teach.note: Geocentric model fitted what people saw. Ptolemy lived in the 2nd century CE. Ask 'Why would people think this?' (it looks that way).

teach.heading: Questions and observations
teach.note: Muslim scholars such as Al-Battani (9th century), who measured the length of the solar year accurately, and Ibn al-Shatir (14th century), who devised improved models for planetary motion. Keep to these facts; do not claim they discovered the heliocentric model.

teach.heading: Sun at the centre
teach.note: Copernicus published in 1543. Galileo observed Jupiter's four large moons in 1610, evidence that not everything orbits Earth.

teach.heading: Science changes with evidence
teach.note: Discuss: why is it good for scientists to change their minds? Link to humility and seeking knowledge: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that whoever treads a path to seek knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise (Sahih Muslim).

practice: What is the difference between geocentric and heliocentric?
What did Galileo see through his telescope?
Why do scientists change their ideas?
independent: Draw the geocentric and heliocentric models side by side with labels.
Write a timeline with four dates and events in astronomy.
Explain in a short paragraph why new evidence is important in science.
exit: Which model has the Sun at the centre?
Name one tool that helped astronomers see further.
lessons.homework: Research one astronomer and write three facts about them.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a timeline with pictures. Stretch: explain why a model can be useful even if it later needs improving.

lessons.title: Gravity and weight
objectives: Explain that gravity is a force that pulls objects towards the Earth
Describe the difference between mass and weight in simple terms
Measure forces using a newton meter

keywords.def: a push or a pull
the force that pulls objects towards each other, such as towards Earth
the unit used to measure force
the force of gravity pulling on an object

starter: Bismillah. Name one thing that orbits the Sun.
What is a force?
What happens when you drop a ball?

teach.heading: What is a force?
bullets: A force is a push or a pull
Forces can change shape or direction
teach.note: Ask children to push and pull objects at home. Forces are measured in newtons (N). Introduce the idea of balanced and unbalanced forces briefly.

teach.heading: Gravity
bullets: It keeps us on the ground
It keeps the Moon in orbit
teach.note: Drop two items (a book and a sheet of paper) at home. Misconception: heavier objects fall faster. In a vacuum all fall at the same rate; in air, air resistance matters.

teach.heading: Weight and mass
bullets: Weight is a force measured in newtons
Mass is how much matter there is
On the Moon weight is smaller
teach.note: Gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth of Earth's. Your mass stays the same but your weight changes. Keep to this level at Year 5.

teach.heading: Newton meter
bullets: The scale reads force in N
A 100 g mass weighs about 1 N
teach.note: Safe demo: use a rubber band with a ruler to show stretch, or a video of a newton meter. A 100 g mass weighs about 1 N on Earth. Mention Isaac Newton, after whom the unit is named.

practice: In which direction does gravity pull?
Is weight measured in kilograms or newtons?
Would an astronaut weigh more on Earth or the Moon?
independent: Draw arrows showing the force of gravity on a ball, a box and a falling apple.
Write the difference between weight and mass.
Explain why a feather and a hammer fall at the same rate on the Moon.
exit: What unit do we use to measure force?
lessons.homework: Find three examples at home of gravity at work and draw arrows to show the force.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: demonstrate push and pull with real objects. Stretch: calculate weight from mass using 10 N per kilogram (approximately).

lessons.title: Air resistance
objectives: Explain that air resistance is a force that slows moving objects
Investigate the effect of surface area on falling
Draw force arrows for a parachute

keywords.def: the force of air pushing against a moving object
the size of the outside of an object that meets the air
a canopy that slows a falling object using air resistance
shaped to move easily through air or water

starter: Bismillah. What is gravity?
What unit do we use to measure force?
What happens to a leaf when it falls?

teach.heading: Air pushes back
bullets: Air is made of tiny particles
teach.note: Hold a piece of card flat then push it through the air. Feel the resistance. Link to riding a bike into the wind.

teach.heading: Surface area
bullets: Bigger surface area: more air resistance
teach.note: Compare a flat sheet of paper with a scrunched ball dropped from the same height. Misconception: the ball is heavier. They have the same mass.

teach.heading: Parachutes
bullets: A large canopy has lots of air resistance
teach.note: Draw arrows: gravity down, air resistance up. Safe practical: make a parachute from a plastic bag, string and a small weight such as a toy figure; drop from a safe height (below a metre, indoors) or watch a video.

teach.heading: Fair test
bullets: Keep weight and height the same
teach.note: Time falls over 1.5 m, repeat three times and find the mean if appropriate. Reaction time errors: discuss.

practice: Which falls more slowly: a flat sheet of paper or a scrunched ball?
Draw the two forces acting on a falling parachute.
Why are racing cyclists' helmets streamlined?
independent: Plan a fair test to find out how canopy size affects falling time. Say what you change, measure and keep the same.
Record the results in a table: size (cm), time (seconds), repeat 1 2 3.
Write a conclusion explaining your results using the words air resistance.
exit: Why does a parachute slow a fall?
lessons.homework: Drop a flat and a scrunched piece of paper from the same height and describe what happens.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a results table and force arrow template. Stretch: explain why a skydiver changes body position to change speed.

lessons.title: Water resistance and friction
objectives: Explain water resistance and friction as forces that slow movement
Compare how different surfaces affect friction
Describe where friction is helpful and where it is a problem

keywords.def: a force between two surfaces that slows movement
the force of water pushing against a moving object
how well a surface holds without slipping
a slippery substance that reduces friction

starter: Bismillah. What is air resistance?
Draw the forces on a falling parachute in your head: which way does each arrow point?
What happens when you push a toy car across a carpet and then a floor?

teach.heading: Water resistance
bullets: Water resistance is stronger than air resistance
teach.note: Walk through water compared to air. Show a video of swimmers or a boat hull. Safe demo: pull your hand through a bowl of water.

teach.heading: Friction
teach.note: Rub your hands together and feel warmth. Friction acts opposite to motion. Misconception: friction only happens with rough surfaces; smooth surfaces have friction too, just less.

teach.heading: Useful and unhelpful
teach.note: Ask for examples at home. Link to wiping hands to wash before prayer: wet hands slide more easily, less friction.

teach.heading: Friction investigation
bullets: Push a toy car down a ramp
teach.note: Safe practical at home: a cardboard ramp, a toy car and surfaces such as a towel, paper and a tray. Keep the ramp height constant; record distance in cm; repeat three times.

practice: Name one place where friction is useful.
Which surface will give the most friction: carpet or ice?
Why are boats streamlined?
independent: Record your results in a table and draw a bar chart of distance against surface.
Write a conclusion explaining which surface has the most friction and why.
List three ways to reduce friction and three ways to increase it.
exit: Give an example of water resistance.
lessons.homework: Find three places at home where friction is helpful and one where it is a problem.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use real surfaces on camera. Stretch: explain why a ball slows down and stops even with no one pushing it.

lessons.title: Levers, pulleys and gears
objectives: Describe how levers, pulleys and gears make work easier
Identify simple machines in everyday life
Explain how a force can be magnified

keywords.def: a bar that turns around a pivot to lift or move something
the point a lever turns around
a wheel with a rope that helps lift loads
a toothed wheel that passes on movement

starter: Bismillah. Name two resistive forces that slow things down.
What is friction?
Have you used a seesaw?

teach.heading: Levers
bullets: A lever turns around a pivot
A longer lever needs less force
teach.note: Safe demo: a ruler over a pencil lifts a small stack of coins. A longer handle makes lifting easier. Common misconception: machines do the work for free; they only reduce force by increasing distance.

teach.heading: Pulleys
teach.note: Show a video of a pulley system lifting a load. Ask 'Why is it easier to pull down than push up?'

teach.heading: Gears
teach.note: Show a bicycle. A small gear driven by a large gear turns faster. Provide a short video.

teach.heading: Machines around us
teach.note: Children search their homes for levers, gears, and pulleys (tap handle, door handle, scissors, can opener) and share findings.

practice: Where is the pivot on a seesaw?
Does a longer lever need more force or less force?
Name a device that uses gears.
independent: Draw a lever with a pivot, load and effort labelled.
Find five machines at home and say whether each is a lever, pulley or gear.
Explain how a pulley makes lifting easier.
lessons.homework: Draw a machine from home that uses a lever and explain how it helps.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide labelled diagrams and a video. Stretch: explain why a long spanner turns a stuck nut more easily.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Properties of materials
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is a window made of glass and not wood?
objectives: To understand that materials are chosen for their properties
successCriteria: All: describe materials as hard, transparent, flexible or strong
Most: match a material to a job because of its property
Some: explain why one material is better than another for a job
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: choosing materials for a product
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the variety of materials Allah has placed in the earth

keywords.def: what a material is like, such as hard or bendy
difficult to scratch or dent
lets light through so you can see through it
bends without breaking
does not break easily under a force

hook.text: A teapot made of chocolate, a raincoat made of paper. Why would these be silly? What does that tell us about choosing materials?
hook.a: Chocolate melts and paper soaks up water: materials must have the right properties for the job.

islamicLink.text: Allah says He made for us garments that protect us from the heat (an-Nahl 16:81), and from the wool, fur and hair of animals things we use (an-Nahl 16:80). Choosing the right material for a job is using Allah's gifts wisely.

starter.q: Recap: which force pulls objects towards the Earth?
Recap: how long does the Earth take to spin once?
Recap: which force slows a parachute?

teach.heading: Properties
bullets: A property is what a material is like
Hard or soft, transparent or opaque
Flexible or rigid, strong or weak
teach.note: Hold up a spoon, a sock and a glass on camera. Ask for one property of each.

teach.heading: Material and object
bullets: The material is what it is made of
A spoon can be metal, wood or plastic
teach.note: Common mix-up: 'the material is a cup'. Correct: the cup is made of ceramic.

teach.heading: Match the job
teach.note: Ask for a reason with 'because' each time.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which property matters most for a window?
check.why: We need to see through a window, so it must be transparent.

practice.q: Why are saucepans made of metal?
practice.a: Metal is strong and does not melt on the cooker; it lets heat through to the food.
practice.model:
What is the job?
Cooking on heat.
What property is needed?
It must not melt and must let heat through.
Metal does both.
So saucepans are made of metal.

practice.q: Name a flexible material.
practice.a: For example: rubber, fabric, plastic film.

practice.q: Is glass transparent or opaque?
practice.a: Transparent (clear glass).

independent.q: Core: Choose 6 objects at home. Make a table: object, material, two properties.
independent.a: For example: spoon, steel, hard and strong; sock, cotton, soft and flexible.
independent.model: Teacher does the first: mug, ceramic, hard and waterproof.

independent.q: Extend: For two objects, explain why the material suits the job.
independent.a: For example: a sock is made of cotton because it is soft and flexible, so it is comfortable.

independent.q: Stretch: Suggest a better material for one object and say why.
independent.a: Accept a reasoned answer, e.g. a plastic cup for toddlers: it will not shatter if dropped.

exit.q: A material that bends without breaking is...
exit.a: A) flexible

exit.q: Big question: why is a window made of glass and not wood?
exit.a: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see out; wood is opaque.

lessons.homework: Find three objects made of the same material at home and write the property that makes the material useful for each.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects and a property word bank. EAL: hard, soft, bendy, clear with pictures. Stretch: compare two materials for the same job with two properties each.

Properties table (portal worksheet, printable or on a drawing tablet)
Household objects: spoon, sock, glass, plastic bag, wooden spoon
Science exercise book and pencil

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Testing and ranking materials
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we prove which material is the hardest?
objectives: To understand how to compare materials with simple tests and rank them
successCriteria: All: carry out a scratch or bend test on four materials
Most: rank the materials from most to least
Some: suggest how to make the test fairer
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest recording, even when the result surprises us

keywords.def: a way to find something out
put in order
how difficult it is to scratch
how easily it bends
results that show something is true

hook.text: You think a plastic spoon is harder than a wooden one. How could you prove it without breaking anything?
hook.a: A scratch test: try to scratch each with the same object and compare the marks.

starter.q: What is a property?
starter.a: What a material is like, such as hard or flexible.

starter.q: A window needs to be...
Name a hard material.

teach.heading: Scratch test
bullets: Scratch each material with the same coin
teach.note: Show on camera with soap, wood, plastic and a metal spoon. An adult supervises; no knives.

teach.heading: Bend test
bullets: Bend a strip of each material
Does it spring back, bend or snap?
teach.note: Use paper, card, a plastic ruler and a lolly stick; hold gently.

teach.heading: Rank the results
teach.note: Example scratch test results.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A coin leaves a deep scratch. The material is...
check.why: A deep mark means the material is easy to scratch: soft.

practice.q: From the table, which material is hardest?
practice.a: The metal spoon: no scratch mark.
practice.model:
The hardest material gets the smallest mark.
The metal spoon had no mark.
So it is the hardest.

practice.q: Why must we use the same coin and pressure?
practice.a: To keep the test fair, so only the material changes.

practice.q: A lolly stick snaps when bent. Is it flexible?
practice.a: No, it is rigid and brittle.

independent.q: Core: Do a bend test on four strips (paper, card, plastic ruler, lolly stick). Rank them from most to least flexible.
independent.a: Usually paper, card, plastic ruler, lolly stick.
independent.model: Teacher shows paper first: bends easily, springs back a little: most flexible.

independent.q: Extend: Write a sentence using your evidence: 'The most flexible was ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: The paper was the most flexible because it bent the most without breaking.

independent.q: Stretch: How could you measure flexibility with a number instead of words?
independent.a: For example: hang the same small weight on the end of each strip and measure how far it bends with a ruler.

exit.q: To rank means to...
exit.a: A) put in order

exit.q: Big question: how can we prove which material is the hardest?
exit.a: Do a fair scratch test and compare the marks: the smallest mark is the hardest.

lessons.homework: Rank five materials at home by how well they keep water out (with an adult, use a few drops of water). Record your ranking.
lessons.send: SEND: two materials at a time to compare. EAL: bend, snap, scratch with actions. Stretch: design a fair strength test for carrier bags.

A coin, a bar of soap, wooden and metal spoons, a plastic lid
Strips of paper, card, a plastic ruler and a lolly stick
Science exercise book and pencil

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Thermal conductors and insulators
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do saucepans have plastic or wooden handles?
objectives: To understand that some materials let heat through easily and others do not
successCriteria: All: sort materials into thermal conductors and insulators
Most: carry out the spoon test fairly
Some: explain why pan handles and oven gloves are made of insulators
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: kitchen equipment design
lessons.smsc: Moral: staying safe in the kitchen

keywords.def: a material that lets heat pass through easily
a material that does not let heat pass through easily
to do with heat
energy that makes things warm
move from one place to another

hook.text: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are left in a bowl of hot soup. Which handle would you rather touch, and why?
hook.a: The wooden one: wood is a thermal insulator, so it stays cooler.

starter.q: Which is more flexible: paper or a lolly stick?
What does 'rank' mean?
Name a transparent material.

teach.heading: Heat moves
bullets: Heat moves from hot to cold
Some materials let it through quickly
teach.note: Hold a metal spoon in warm water: the handle warms up. Ask why.

teach.heading: Conductors and insulators
teach.note: Sort as a class.

teach.heading: The spoon test
bullets: Spoons of different materials in a mug of warm water
Same size, same depth, same time
teach.note: An adult pours warm (not hot) tap water. Touch gently.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

options: They are insulators that slow heat
check.why: The padding is a thermal insulator, so heat reaches your hand slowly.

practice.q: Is copper a thermal conductor or insulator?
practice.a: A conductor (it is a metal).
practice.model:
Is it a metal?
Yes.
Metals let heat through easily.
So copper is a thermal conductor.

practice.q: Why do pans have plastic handles?
practice.a: Plastic is an insulator, so the handle stays cool enough to hold.

practice.q: Which handle got warm in the test?
practice.a: The metal one.

independent.q: Core: Do the spoon test with an adult (metal, plastic and wooden spoons in warm water). Record how each handle feels after 3 minutes.
independent.a: Metal: warm; plastic and wood: cool.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: same mug, all spoons in together, start the timer, wait 3 minutes before touching.

independent.q: Extend: Write a conclusion using 'conductor' and 'insulator'.
independent.a: The metal spoon is a thermal conductor because its handle warmed up; plastic and wood are insulators.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do houses have loft insulation made of fluffy material?
independent.a: It traps air, a good insulator, so heat escapes slowly from the house.

exit.q: Metals are good thermal...
exit.a: A) conductors

exit.q: Big question: why do saucepans have plastic or wooden handles?
exit.a: They are insulators, so heat does not reach your hand quickly.

lessons.homework: Find three thermal insulators and three conductors in your kitchen. Say what each is used for.
lessons.send: SEND: feel test with an adult and smiley scale. EAL: hot, warm, cool, conductor, insulator. Stretch: rank four materials as insulators.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Magnetic materials and electrical conductors
lessons.bigQuestion: Are all good conductors of heat also magnetic?
objectives: To understand that materials can be grouped by more than one property, such as magnetism and electrical conductivity
successCriteria: All: test materials with a magnet
Most: say that metals conduct electricity and only some metals are magnetic
Some: use two properties to sort materials in a table
lessons.smsc: Social: safety with electricity at home

keywords.def: pulled by a magnet
a material that lets electricity flow through it
a material that does not let electricity flow
a material such as iron, copper or aluminium
sort into groups

hook.text: Copper wires carry electricity in your walls, yet a magnet does not pull copper. What does that tell you?
hook.a: Conducting and being magnetic are different properties; copper conducts but is not magnetic.

starter.q: Is wood a thermal conductor or insulator?
Name a magnetic metal.
Why do pans have plastic handles?

teach.heading: Magnetic materials
bullets: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic
teach.note: Recap from Year 3: aluminium and copper are not magnetic.

teach.heading: Electrical conductors
bullets: Plastic, wood, rubber and glass do not
teach.note: Never test mains electricity. Show a picture of a cut cable: copper core, plastic coat.

teach.heading: Two properties
teach.note: Read each card.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which is an electrical conductor but NOT magnetic?
check.why: Copper is a metal so it conducts, but it is not magnetic.

practice.q: Is aluminium magnetic? Does it conduct electricity?
practice.a: Not magnetic; it does conduct electricity.
practice.model:
Two questions, two answers.
Magnetic?
Aluminium is not.
Conducts?
It is a metal and all metals conduct.
So: not magnetic, but a conductor.

practice.q: Why are wires coated in plastic?
practice.a: Plastic is an electrical insulator, so it keeps us safe.

practice.q: Which metals are magnetic?
practice.a: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.

independent.q: Core: Test 8 household items with a magnet. Then use the table rule (metals conduct) to fill in a second column. Never test plugs or sockets.
independent.a: Pupils' own; steel items magnetic; all metal items conduct; plastic, wood, fabric do not.
independent.model: Teacher shows the first: steel spoon: magnetic yes; metal, so conducts yes.

independent.q: Extend: Which of your materials was a conductor but not magnetic?
independent.a: For example: aluminium foil or a copper coin.

independent.q: Stretch: Why might a recycling plant use a magnet and then another method to sort metals?
independent.a: The magnet removes steel; aluminium and copper are not magnetic so need another method.

exit.q: All metals...
exit.a: B) conduct electricity

exit.q: Big question: are all good conductors of heat also magnetic?
exit.a: No: copper and aluminium conduct heat well but are not magnetic.

lessons.homework: Draw a two-way table of six objects at home: magnetic or not, conductor or not. Never test sockets or plugs.
lessons.send: SEND: yes/no cards for each column. EAL: conduct, insulate, magnetic. Stretch: add thermal conductor as a third column.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Choosing the best insulator for a warm drink
lessons.bigQuestion: Which material would keep your drink warm the longest?
objectives: To understand how to plan a fair test to find the best thermal insulator
successCriteria: All: make a prediction about the best insulator
Most: name the variable to change, keep the same and measure
Some: explain why the starting temperature must be the same
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah's gifts of wool and fur that keep creatures and people warm

keywords.def: a material that slows down heat loss
something that can change in a test
right for the job
how hot or cold something is
what we think will happen

hook.text: You wrap one cup of warm water in a woolly scarf and one in foil. Which stays warm longer? Why?
hook.a: Usually the wool: it traps air, a good insulator. Test it to find out.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And the grazing livestock He has created for you; in them is warmth and many benefits' (an-Nahl 16:5). Wool from sheep is one of the best natural insulators.

starter.q: A material that slows heat is a thermal...
Which spoon handle got warm?
In a fair test we change...

teach.heading: Our question
bullets: Which wrapping keeps warm water warm longest?
Wrappings: wool, foil, paper towel, bubble wrap
One cup with no wrapping to compare
teach.note: The bare cup is the 'control'.

teach.heading: Variables
bullets: Keep the same: cup, water amount, start temperature, place
teach.note: Ask pupils to name each one.

teach.heading: Safety
teach.note: Read the safety card together.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.why: We change the wrapping; the amount of water must stay the same.

practice.q: Write a prediction: 'I think ... will keep the water warmest because ...'
practice.a: For example: I think wool will keep the water warmest because it traps air.
practice.model:
Choose a material.
Give a reason using what you know.
Wool traps air.
Air is an insulator.
So: 'I think wool will be best because it traps air, which is an insulator.'

practice.q: Why have a cup with no wrapping?
practice.a: To compare: it shows how fast the water cools without insulation.

practice.q: What will we measure?
practice.a: The temperature of the water after 20 minutes.

independent.q: Core: Set up your test: 3 wrapped cups and 1 bare cup with the same warm water. Record the start temperature (or feel test) and leave them for 20 minutes.
independent.a: Pupils' own set-up; the start temperature recorded for each cup.
independent.model: Teacher shows one cup first: measure 100 ml of warm water, wrap with wool, secure with a band, record the start temperature.

independent.q: Extend: Write your plan as 4 numbered steps.
independent.a: 1 Pour the same water into each cup. 2 Wrap three cups. 3 Measure the start temperature. 4 Measure again after 20 minutes.

independent.q: Stretch: Why must all cups start at the same temperature?
independent.a: So the only difference is the wrapping; otherwise a hotter cup would stay warm longer anyway.

exit.q: The thing we change is the...
exit.a: A) wrapping

exit.q: Big question: which material would keep your drink warm the longest?
exit.a: Our prediction is the wool; we will check with the results next lesson.

lessons.homework: Finish your test and record the final temperatures (or feel test scores) in the results table for next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: a planning frame with picture prompts. EAL: change, same, measure, predict. Stretch: add a fifth material and predict where it ranks.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Science Long Term Plan 2023-24, Year 5 Spring (Cornerstones Alchemy Island)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Presenting results: bar charts and conclusions
lessons.bigQuestion: What does our bar chart tell us about the best insulator?
objectives: To understand how to present results in a bar chart and use them to write a conclusion
successCriteria: All: draw a bar for each material
Most: read the chart to find the best insulator
Some: write a conclusion that uses numbers from the chart
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: drawing and reading bar charts with a scale
lessons.smsc: Moral: reporting results honestly, even if our prediction was wrong

keywords.def: a chart with bars to compare amounts
the line along the side or bottom of a chart
what the results tell us
what we found out
a material that slows heat transfer

hook.text: If your prediction was wrong, does that mean your test failed?
hook.a: No. A test that shows our prediction was wrong still teaches us something true.

starter.q: What did we change in the insulation test?
Why have a bare cup?
starter.a: To compare with the wrapped cups.

starter.q: Is wool a conductor or insulator?

teach.heading: Example results
bullets: Higher temperature means less heat lost
teach.note: Example data from a class test, start 50 °C, after 20 minutes.

teach.heading: Drawing a bar chart
bullets: Use a ruler; label both axes
teach.note: Model the first bar on squared paper.

teach.heading: Writing a conclusion
teach.note: Model: The wool was the best insulator: the water was still 45 °C. Wool traps air, which slows heat loss.

model.problem: Write a conclusion from the chart.
steps: Explain: wool traps air, an insulator
model.answer: Wool was the best insulator (45 °C after 20 minutes, against 36 °C with no wrapping) because it traps air.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which was the worst insulator of the wrappings?
check.why: Foil kept the lowest temperature (39 °C) of the wrapped cups.

practice.q: How much warmer was the wool cup than the bare cup?
practice.a: 45 - 36 = 9 °C warmer.
practice.model:
Read both bars: wool 45, bare 36.
Subtract: 45 - 36 = 9.
So the wool cup was 9 °C warmer.

practice.q: Put the materials in order, best insulator first.
practice.a: Wool, bubble wrap, paper towel, foil.

practice.q: What goes on the side (vertical) axis?
practice.a: Temperature in °C.

independent.q: Core: Draw a bar chart of your own results (or the class example) with labelled axes.
independent.a: A bar chart with materials on the horizontal axis and temperature in °C on the vertical axis.
independent.model: Teacher draws the first bar: bare cup, up to 36 on the scale, ruler, shade it in.

independent.q: Extend: Write a conclusion with numbers in the portal response box. Start: 'The best insulator was ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: The best insulator was wool because the water stayed at 45 °C, 9 °C warmer than the bare cup.

independent.q: Stretch: Was your prediction correct? How could you make the test more reliable?
independent.a: Pupils' own; repeat the test and take an average.

exit.q: The best insulator kept the water...
exit.a: A) hottest

exit.q: Big question: what does our bar chart tell us about the best insulator?
exit.a: The tallest bar shows the best insulator: wool in the example.

lessons.homework: Explain your bar chart to someone at home and ask them which material they would use for a lunch bag.
lessons.send: SEND: a chart with the scale drawn already. EAL: bar, axis, highest, lowest. Stretch: work out the temperature drop for each material.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Habitats and microhabitats around the home
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do woodlice live under logs and not on sunny walls?
objectives: To understand that habitats provide living things with what they need
successCriteria: All: name a habitat and a microhabitat
Most: say what a habitat provides (food, water, shelter)
Some: explain why an animal is found in one microhabitat and not another
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: different habitats across the world
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah provides for every creature in its home

keywords.def: the natural home of a living thing
a very small habitat, such as under a stone
the surroundings of a living thing
a safe place from weather and predators
how damp, dark, warm or cold a place is

hook.text: A garden has a sunny wall, a damp log and a pond. Which creatures might live in each, and why?
hook.a: Lizards or bees on the warm wall, woodlice under the damp log, pond snails in the water: each place gives them what they need.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its wings, except that they are communities like you' (al-An'am 6:38). Every habitat is home to a community of living things that Allah created and provides for.

starter.q: Which was the best insulator in our example?
Name a living thing in your garden or park.
starter.a: For example: a worm, a bird, a tree.

starter.q: What do all animals need to live?

teach.heading: Habitats
bullets: A habitat is a living thing's home
It gives food, water and shelter
teach.note: Ask pupils to name a habitat they have seen.

teach.heading: Microhabitats
bullets: Tiny habitats inside a bigger one
Under a log, in a crack, under a leaf
teach.note: Each has its own conditions.

teach.heading: Being kind to minibeasts
bullets: Lift a log gently, put it back
teach.note: Adab: Allah made these creatures; we disturb them as little as possible.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Where would you most likely find woodlice?
check.why: Woodlice need damp, dark conditions or they dry out.

practice.q: Why do worms live in soil?
practice.a: It is damp and dark, and has food (dead leaves); it protects them.
practice.model:
List what a worm needs: damp, dark, food.
Does soil give these?
Yes.
So soil is a good habitat for worms.

practice.q: What is a microhabitat?
practice.a: A very small habitat, such as under a stone.

practice.q: Name one thing a habitat provides.
practice.a: Food, water or shelter.

independent.q: Core: With an adult, explore two microhabitats near your home (a plant pot, under a stone, a hedge). Record conditions and any living things.
independent.a: Pupils' own observations, e.g. under a stone: damp, dark, woodlice.
independent.model:
Teacher shows one record: 'Under a plant pot: damp, dark, cool.
Found: 3 woodlice, 1 slug.'

independent.q: Extend: Choose one creature you found and explain how the microhabitat meets its needs.
independent.a: For example: woodlice need damp; under the pot is damp and dark, so they do not dry out.

independent.q: Stretch: Predict what would happen to the woodlice if the stone were moved into the sun.
independent.a: They would move away to find damp shade or they could dry out.

exit.q: A habitat is...
exit.a: A) a living thing's home

exit.q: Big question: why do woodlice live under logs and not on sunny walls?
exit.a: Under logs it is damp and dark, which they need; sunny walls are too dry.

lessons.homework: Draw a map of one outdoor space near your home and mark three microhabitats.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of minibeasts to match to habitats. EAL: damp, dark, dry, shelter. Stretch: compare two microhabitats in a table.

Microhabitat record sheet (portal worksheet)
Gardening gloves and a magnifying glass if available

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Adaptation: suited to a habitat
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a camel live in the desert but a polar bear cannot?
objectives: To understand that living things have features that suit them to their habitat
successCriteria: All: name a feature of an animal or plant that helps it survive
Most: link the feature to the conditions of its habitat
Some: explain why an animal could not survive in a very different habitat
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: deserts, rainforests and polar regions
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the wisdom in how Allah designed each creature for its home

keywords.def: a feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat
a part or quality of a living thing
stay alive
the surroundings of a living thing
colours that help hide a living thing

hook.text: A cactus has spines instead of flat leaves. Why might that help it in a desert?
hook.a: Spines lose less water than flat leaves and stop animals eating it.

islamicLink.text: Allah asks: 'Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?' (al-Ghashiyah 88:17). The camel's features suit the desert perfectly; Muslims reflect on this as a sign of Allah's wisdom.

starter.q: Woodlice like conditions that are...
What is a microhabitat?
Name a habitat.

teach.heading: Adaptations
teach.note: Introduce with the cactus from the ponder.

teach.heading: The camel
bullets: Wide feet: do not sink in sand
teach.note: Common error: the hump stores water. It stores fat.

misconception.wrong: A camel's hump is full of water
misconception.right: The hump stores fat, which gives energy when food is scarce

teach.heading: Match the feature
teach.note: Read each card.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Why does a duck have webbed feet?
check.why: Webbed feet push against the water like paddles.

practice.q: Why does a polar bear have thick fur?
practice.a: To keep warm in the freezing Arctic.
practice.model:
What is the habitat like?
Very cold.
What does the bear need?
Warmth.
Thick fur traps warm air.
So thick fur keeps it warm.

practice.q: What is camouflage?
practice.a: Colours that help a living thing hide.

practice.q: Why would a camel struggle in the Arctic?
practice.a: It is adapted to heat, not freezing cold and snow.

independent.q: Core: Choose a habitat (desert, pond, woodland or polar). Pick one animal and one plant and list two adaptations each.
independent.a: For example: desert: camel (wide feet, stores fat), cactus (spines, thick waxy stem).
independent.model: Teacher does one first: pond, duck: webbed feet (swimming), waterproof feathers (stays dry).

independent.q: Extend: Explain one adaptation in full: feature, condition, how it helps.
independent.a: For example: A cactus has spines instead of leaves because the desert is dry; spines lose less water.

independent.q: Stretch: Design an imaginary animal for a cold, windy mountain and explain three adaptations (no drawing of people).
independent.a: Accept reasoned features, e.g. thick fur, short ears, strong grip.

exit.q: A feature that helps survival is an...
exit.a: A) adaptation

exit.q: Big question: why can a camel live in the desert but a polar bear cannot?
exit.a: Each is adapted to its own habitat: the camel to heat and dryness, the bear to cold.

lessons.homework: Find one plant at home or in a park. Write two of its features and how they might help it survive.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards of animals and features. EAL: feature, survive, adapt with pictures. Stretch: compare adaptations of two desert animals.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Food chains: producers and consumers
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the energy in a fox's dinner really come from?
objectives: To understand that food chains show how energy passes from producers to consumers
successCriteria: All: write a food chain with arrows
Most: label producer, prey, predator
Some: explain what would happen if one living thing in the chain disappeared
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: food chains in local habitats
lessons.smsc: Moral: our responsibility (amanah) to protect the balance of nature

keywords.def: a living thing that makes its own food, such as a plant
a living thing that eats other living things
an animal that hunts other animals
an animal that is hunted
shows what eats what, with arrows

hook.text: A fox eats a rabbit, and the rabbit eats grass. Where did the energy start?
hook.a: With the Sun: the grass uses sunlight to make food.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And the heaven He raised and He set up the balance, so that you do not transgress the balance' (ar-Rahman 55:7-8). Food chains are part of this balance; harming one creature can affect many others.

starter.q: A cactus's spines are an...
Why does a polar bear have thick fur?
What do plants need to grow?
starter.a: Light, water, air, warmth and nutrients.

teach.heading: Food chains
teach.note: Model: grass → rabbit → fox. Arrow points to the eater.

teach.heading: Producers and consumers
bullets: Producers: plants make their own food
Every chain starts with a producer
teach.note: Ask: why must every chain start with a plant?

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Arrows show the direction of energy
teach.note: Arrows do not point to the food.

misconception.wrong: fox → rabbit (the fox eats the rabbit)
misconception.right: rabbit → fox (energy goes from rabbit to fox)

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: In leaf → caterpillar → bird, which is the producer?
check.why: The leaf is a plant: it makes its own food.

practice.q: Write a food chain: lettuce, slug, thrush.
practice.a: lettuce → slug → thrush
practice.model:
Start with the producer: lettuce.
What eats it?
Slug.
What eats the slug?
Thrush.
Arrows point to the eater: lettuce → slug → thrush.

practice.q: In that chain, which is the predator?
practice.a: The thrush.

practice.q: What does the arrow mean?
practice.a: 'Is eaten by': energy passes along it.

independent.q: Core: Write three food chains from a woodland, a pond and the sea. Label producer, prey and predator.
independent.a: For example: acorn → squirrel → fox; pondweed → tadpole → heron; seaweed → limpet → crab.
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first: oak leaf → caterpillar → blue tit.
Producer: oak leaf.
Prey: caterpillar.
Predator: blue tit.

independent.q: Extend: In grass → rabbit → fox, what happens if the rabbits disappear?
independent.a: Foxes have less food and may decrease; grass may grow more.

independent.q: Stretch: Why are there usually fewer predators than prey?
independent.a: Energy is used up at each step, so less is passed on to the predators.

exit.q: Every food chain starts with a...
exit.a: A) producer

exit.q: Big question: where does the energy in a fox's dinner really come from?
exit.a: From the Sun, through the grass and then the rabbit.

lessons.homework: Write a food chain for one meal you ate today, starting with a plant.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards to order with arrow cards. EAL: eat, eaten by, producer, predator. Stretch: join two chains into a food web.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Properties of materials and habitats (Alchemy Island and Living Things and Their Habitats)
lessons.title: Classifying living things: vertebrates, invertebrates and plants
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a snail more like a worm or like a fish?
objectives: To understand how living things are grouped by their features
successCriteria: All: sort animals into vertebrates and invertebrates
Most: name the five vertebrate groups
Some: sort plants into flowering and non-flowering with a reason
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the variety of Allah's creation

keywords.def: sort into groups by features
an animal with a backbone
an animal without a backbone
a plant that makes flowers and seeds
a plant without flowers, such as a fern or moss

hook.text: A whale lives in the sea like a fish. Is it a fish? How could you decide?
hook.a: No: it breathes air with lungs and feeds its young milk, so it is a mammal.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Allah has created every animal from water. Of them are some that creep on their bellies, some that walk on two legs, and some that walk on four' (an-Nur 24:45). The Qur'an itself groups animals by how they move.

starter.q: Write a food chain with grass, rabbit and fox.
A plant is a...
What is an adaptation?
starter.a: A feature that helps a living thing survive.

teach.heading: Backbone or not?
teach.note: Feel your own spine: that is a backbone.

teach.heading: Five vertebrate groups
teach.note: One feature each.

head: Group
Key feature
Example
rows: fur or hair; feed young milk
moist skin; live in water and on land

teach.heading: Sort the animals
teach.note: Read each card.

teach.heading: Plants too
teach.note: Ferns and mosses make spores; conifers make cones.

practice.q: Is a spider a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
practice.a: An invertebrate: it has no backbone.
practice.model:
Ask: does it have a backbone?
A spider does not; it has a hard outer skeleton.
No backbone means invertebrate.

practice.q: Which vertebrate group has feathers?
practice.a: Birds.

practice.q: Is a fern a flowering plant?
practice.a: No, it is non-flowering (it makes spores).

independent.q: Core: Sort 12 living things (from the portal card set) into vertebrates (in their five groups), invertebrates and plants.
independent.a: Answers on the card set key, e.g. whale: mammal; frog: amphibian; snail: invertebrate; fern: non-flowering plant.
independent.model: Teacher sorts the first two: robin (feathers: bird), earthworm (no backbone: invertebrate).

independent.q: Extend: Why is a whale a mammal and not a fish?
independent.a: It breathes air with lungs and feeds its young milk.

independent.q: Stretch: Write three yes/no questions that would sort any vertebrate into its group.
independent.a: For example: Does it have feathers? Does it have fur? Does it have gills?

exit.q: An animal with a backbone is a...
exit.a: A) vertebrate

exit.q: Big question: is a snail more like a worm or like a fish?
exit.a: Like a worm: both are invertebrates with no backbone.

lessons.homework: Find five living things near your home and classify each one (vertebrate group, invertebrate or plant).
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards with one question at a time. EAL: backbone, feathers, scales, fur. Stretch: research one invertebrate group (insects, spiders, molluscs).
